claims.text: Single-phase high-entropy alloys can undergo rapid ductility loss and early failure at intermediate temperatures of approximately 400–800°C.
High-strain-rate deformation at 400–800°C causes extensive shear-driven dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement.
The deformation produces a nanocrystalline network with grain sizes of approximately 10–50 nm.
The dynamically produced grain-boundary network consists predominantly of high-angle, high-energy boundaries.
Below a critical grain size, plastic deformation shifts from dislocation-mediated slip to grain-boundary sliding.
High-angle grain boundaries in the refined alloy have reduced cohesive strength and are susceptible to localized cohesive failure.
Grain-boundary sliding and weakened boundary cohesion cause intergranular decohesion during tensile loading.
The proposed decohesion mechanism can operate without significant grain-boundary segregation or phase separation.
The brittle response is governed by the refined boundary network rather than conventional impurity segregation or brittle grain-boundary precipitation.
Relative to the coarse-grained baseline, dynamic refinement markedly reduces ductility and toughness.
Fracture after dynamic refinement will exhibit predominantly intergranular decohesion.
Dynamic refinement reduces strain hardening relative to the initial coarse-grained state.
Brittle failure begins earlier despite the alloy retaining inherently high strength.
The initial coarse-grained homogeneous alloy has favorable toughness and ductility and deforms primarily by dislocation slip.
Lower temperatures suppress dynamic grain refinement and therefore suppress the proposed decohesion mechanism.
At temperatures above the intermediate range, diffusion-driven boundary relaxation can mitigate decohesion.
Inert or ultra-high-vacuum conditions prevent oxidation and impurity segregation sufficiently to isolate the intrinsic grain-boundary mechanism.
